Discover Board Game Arena Rules summary Contents 1 Objective 2 Quick Setup 3 Gameplay 3.1 Action 1: Play & Place 3.2 Action 2: Pass & Refresh 4 Key Decision Information 4.1 The 5 Combination Types 4.2 Climbing Rules (Beating Combinations) 4.3 Joker Rules 5 Game End Objective In Lepidoptery , a hybrid of a connection game and a deck climber, there are two ways to win: Four in a Row: Be the first to connect four of your tokens in a vertical, horizontal, or diagonal line. Shed Out: Be the first to play all the cards from your hand and your deck. Quick Setup Decks: Each player has a 38-card deck (ranks 1-10) and starts with a 12-card hand . Joker: Each player has one Joker (wildcard) placed face up in front of them. Board: Place the board between players. Each column represents one of the five combination types. Gameplay Players take turns choosing one of the following two actions: Action 1: Play & Place This action allows you to play cards and place tokens on the board. Play a Combination: Play a valid card combination from your hand. Restriction: You cannot play the same combination type twice in a row (unless you passed in between). Placeable: There must be an empty space in the corresponding column on the board. Climbing: Your combination must "beat" the previous one (see Climbing Rules below). Place Token: "Drop" a token into the lowest empty space of the column matching your combination. Update Marker: Move your marker to show which combination type you just played. Check for Win: Check if you have achieved "Four in a Row" or "Shed Out". Clear Columns: If your token fills a column, remove all tokens from all other already full columns. Action 2: Pass & Refresh Choose this if you cannot or do not want to play (not allowed if you are the leader and have a legal move). Clear Play Area: Discard all cards currently in the play area. Pass Marker: Move your marker to the "Pass" slot. Reset Joker: Flip your Joker back to its face-up (active) side. Draw Cards: All players replenish their hands to 12 cards . If a player already has 12 or more cards, they draw exactly one card instead. Key Decision Information The 5 Combination Types Single: One card (e.g., 7). Pair: Two cards of the same rank (e.g., 6-6). Run of 2: Two cards with sequential ranks (e.g., 4-5). Triple: Three cards of the same rank (e.g., 8-8-8). Run of 3: Three cards with sequential ranks (e.g., 1-2-3). Climbing Rules (Beating Combinations) A new combination beats the previous one if: Its lowest card rank is higher than the lowest rank of the previous combo. OR: The lowest rank is the same, but the new combo contains more cards (e.g., a Pair of 5s beats a Single 5). Note: Combinations belonging to the same column (type) cannot be played on each other. Joker Rules Jokers are Wildcards (ranks 1-10) but cannot be played as a Single . Once played, flip the Joker over. It only refreshes when you take the "Pass & Refresh" action. Jokers are not part of your deck and do not need to be played to "Shed Out". Game End The game ends immediately when a player completes a line of four tokens or plays their final card from both hand and deck. [Rating: 1/10] After playing it more, I still kinda like it, but feel like it's too exhausting and limiting to play repeatedly. Like sometimes the board gets jammed up, so we have no need to play strategically anymore, and then you're just playing a too-generous climber. It feels more disconnected from the card play than it wants to be. But when the board gets high-stakes, then it's all about getting those 2 turns in a row, and then it's over instantly. Something about the arc feels disjointed. But it's still clever and will amuse a new player on the first try.

[Rating: 3/10] 2025-12-11, 4/10 @ 4 plays:  I hate connect four. I hate it even more when your opponents can play twice in a row because they happened to draw higher cards. All my plays have devolved into stalemates where someone draws well enough to play two high card combos in a row to win. Good idea in there somewhere, maybe.

[Rating: 3/10] A 2p card shedding game where players are playing connect 4 via trick taking. Players take turns playing stronger melds to beat the card(s) last played, they may not play the same meld. Strength of a meld is simply determinedly the lowest card of that meld, a 10 beats a meld of 8,9,10. The type of meld played will dictate which piece is dropped into the connect 4 grid. Once a player passes, player(s) draw back up to hand size and begins playing cards again. Players win if they shed their hand or produce a 4 in a row.

[Rating: 5/10] Could go up or down with additional plays. Initial impression was not favorable as it took some time to get my mind around not being able to play the same type of set/run twice in a row and that you always have to play a set that has a card that is higher than the current set/run.  Standard Connect 4 strategies don't quite come into play here as it's a smaller grid - I suspect it's more about making your opponent pass so that you can get 'turns in a row" if you will.  I suspect it will often be better to play high cards to try and force them to pass when possible.

[Rating: 5/10] This feels to me more like a game that uses climbing/shedding than a climbing/shedding game. It doesn't have the feel that I'm looking for.  The game does seem to have a decent level of strategy as you try to manage your deck and hand while manipulating the board. The best way to win is set yourself up for consecutive turns by playing melds that your opponent can't beat. You want to use your wild for higher cards and pass to recover it.  I would definitely play this if asked, but I don't see myself asking to play it.  See my thoughts about other climbing/shedding games in my [geeklist=342159][
